fetched_contents.text: Efficacy and safety of carbon ion radiotherapy for bone sarcomas: a systematic review and meta-analysis Abstract Objective This study aimed to systematically evaluate and conduct a meta-analysis of the efficacy and safety of carbon ion radiotherapy for bone sarcomas. Methods We searched for articles using the PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, and the Web of Science databases from their inception to January 12, 2022. Two researchers independently screened the literature and extracted data based on the inclusion and exclusion criteria. Statistical analyses were performed using STATA version 14.0. Results We searched for 4378 candidate articles, of which 12 studies were included in our study according to the inclusion and exclusion criteria. Of the 897 BSs patients who received carbon ion radiotherapy in the studies, 526 patients had chordoma, 255 patients had chondrosarcoma, 112 patients had osteosarcoma, and 4 patients had other sarcomas. The local control rate at 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 10 years in these studies were 98.5% (95% confidence interval [CI] = 0.961–1.009, I2 = 0%), 85.8% (95% CI = 0.687–1.030, I2 = 91%), 86% (95% CI = 0.763–0.957, I2 = 85.3%), 91.1% (95% CI = 0.849–0.974), 74.3% (95% CI = 0.666–0.820, I2 = 85.2%), and 64.7% (95% CI = 0.451–0.843, I2 = 95.3%), respectively. The overall survival rate at 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 10 years in these studies were 99.9% (95% CI = 0.995–1.004, I2 = 0%), 89.6% (95% CI = 0.811–0.980, I2 = 96.6%), 85% (95% CI = 0.750–0.950, I2 = 89.4%), 92.4% (95% CI = 0.866–0.982), 72.7% (95% CI = 0.609–0.844, I2 = 95.3%), and 72.1% (95% CI = 0.661–0.781, I2 = 46.5%), respectively. Across all studies, the incidence of acute and late toxicities was mainly grade 1 to grade 2, and grade 1 to grade 3, respectively. Conclusion As an advanced radiotherapy, carbon ion radiotherapy is promising for patients with bone sarcomas that are unresectable or residual after incomplete surgery. The data indicated that carbon ion radiotherapy was safe and effective for bone sarcomas, showing promising results for local control, overall survival, and lower acute and late toxicity. BSs include osteosarcomas, chondrosarcomas, and chordomas. The traditional treatment for sarcomas is aggressive surgery; upon R0 resection, local recurrence (LR) incidence at 5 years has been reported in 6% of patients [1–3]. However, the complete resection of some sarcomas might not be possible in patients with anatomical complexity; the R2 resection LR rate at 5 years has been reported as 38% [1–4]. In this case, radiotherapy (RT) is an important potential treatment strategy for some patients who have sarcomas that are unresectable or residual after incomplete surgery [5, 6]. Most types of BSs are known to be resistant to radiation, requiring higher dose irradiation to gain adequate local control (LC) [3]. However, traditional radiation therapy, such as photon therapy, has a limited ability to achieve lethal dose irradiation due to the proximity of some sarcomas to organs at risk. In the recent years, advanced radiation modalities including protons and carbon ions have been developed. They can deposit a dose in the “Bragg peak” region providing a more favorable dose-distribution compared to photons, which can deliver a higher dose to the tumor area, while protecting the surrounding tissues and organs. In addition, they have a significant relative biological effectiveness (RBE), especially carbon ions, which exert a greater killing effect on tumor cells than protons. As one of the more advanced radiotherapy modalities, carbon ion radiotherapy (C-ion RT) is a promising treatment strategy for sarcomas [7]. In Japan, C-ion RT was carried out in 1994 for treating all kinds of cancer, including various unresectable BSs [7]. For a long time, the clinical studies of carbon ion therapy for BSs have been mainly reported in case series; however, the sample size was small, and the efficacy and safety were not clear and definite. fetched_contents.text: Five-Year Survival Outcomes After Carbon-Ion Radiotherapy for Operable Stage I NSCLC: A Japanese National Registry Study (J-CROS-LUNG) Introduction The standard therapy for operable stage I NSCLC is surgery.1 Nevertheless, some patients refuse this option and undergo radiotherapy, particularly stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) with radiographs. SBRT results in excellent local control without severe toxicity.2, 3, 4 Carbon-ion radiotherapy (CIRT) is a type of radiotherapy that has physical and biological advantages compared with radiographs.5 Single-institute studies report favorable outcomes for CIRT as a treatment for early stage lung cancer.6, 7, 8, 9 Although the number of facilities capable of CIRT has increased worldwide, Japan has the largest number.10 The Japanese prospective nationwide registry study on CIRT for lung cancer began in 2016. All institutions that perform CIRT as a treatment for NSCLC in Japan participate in this registry. Data from this nationwide registry study have been used to evaluate the effects of CIRT for inoperable patients with stage I NSCLC11 and concomitant interstitial lung diseases.12 Here, we analyzed the real-world clinical outcomes of CIRT for operable patients with stage I NSCLC. Materials and Methods Study Design and Patients This multicenter, prospective, observational registry study was conducted by the Japan Carbon-Ion Radiation Oncology Study Group (J-CROS), which includes all seven current CIRT facilities in Japan. The following five institutions participated: SAGA-HIMAT Foundation (HIMAT, Saga), National Institutes for Quantum and Radiological Science and Technology (QST, Chiba), Ion Beam Therapy Center, Hyogo Ion Beam Medical Center (HIBMC, Hyogo), Gunma University Heavy Ion Medical Center (GHMC, Gunma), and ion beam Radiation Oncology Center in Kanagawa (i-ROCK, Kanagawa). The other two institutions did not participate because they did not use CIRT as a treatment for NSCLC before 2018. All patients with operable stage I NSCLC treated with CIRT in Japan in or after May 2016 (May 2016– June 2018) were enrolled. Clinical stage was evaluated using the TNM Classification of Malignant Tumors, Eighth Edition.13 Patients able to undergo lobectomy were defined as operable by the multidisciplinary tumor board at each institute. The Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events version 5.0 were used to assess toxicity.14 All patients provided written informed consent to participate. This study was performed by the Lung Cancer Working Group in the Particle Beam Therapy Committee and Subcommittee at Japanese Society for Radiation Oncology (JASTRO) and was registered in the UMIN Clinical Trials Registry as UMIN000024709. Treatment The CIRT schedules used were approved by JASTRO.15 Patients received a total dose of 50 Gy (relative biological effectiveness [RBE]) administered in a single fraction, 54 to 64 Gy (RBE) administered in four fractions, or 64 to 72 Gy (RBE) administered in 12 to 16 fractions; the latter was chosen when irradiation with 1 to 4 fractions was difficult owing to the dose constraints of normal organs. Patients with endobronchial lung cancer had the option of receiving 54 Gy (RBE) in nine fractions. CIRT was performed in accordance with the protocols used at each institution. The parameters for the target volume, setup margins, and the dose constraints for organs at risk were determined as per each protocol. Typically, the clinical target volume was defined as the gross target volume plus 0 to 5 mm. Setting of the internal margin accounted for respiratory movement in each direction, as determined by a four-dimensional computed tomography scan. Finally, the planning target volume (PTV) was set by adding the internal and setup margins to the clinical target volume. The lymph node area was not irradiated. The unit used for the prescribed dose of carbon-ion radiotherapy is the Gy (RBE), which is defined as the physical dose (Gy) multiplied by the RBE value for carbon ions.16 The RBE models used in Japan are the mixed beam model or the microdosimetric kinetic model.17 In principle, the passive method delivered the prescribed dose to the isocenter of the PTV, adjusted to cover the PTV with a 95% isodose line, whereas the scanning method delivered the prescribed dose to 95% of the volume of the PTV. All institutions used daily image-guided radiotherapy with orthogonal two-dimensional kV image pairs, and some also used computed tomography. Statistical Analysis The definitions were as follows: overall survival (OS) is the time from the start of CIRT to the last follow-up date or death (non–lung cancer-related death was treated as censored in cause-specific survival [CSS] analysis); progression-free survival (PFS) was defined as the time from the start of CIRT to the last follow-up date, death, or any recurrence; the local control rate (LC) was defined as the time from the start of CIRT to the time of the last follow-up or local recurrence. Any recurrence, apart from local recurrence, was censored during LC analysis. Diagnosis of local recurrence was made by imaging, without biopsy. OS, CSS, PFS, and LC were estimated using the Kaplan–Meier method, and differences between subgroups were evaluated using the log-rank test. Receiver operating characteristic curve analysis was performed to determine optimal cutoff values. Prognostic factors were evaluated or identified by a Cox proportional hazards model. Fisher’s exact test was used to compare recurrence rates between two groups. All statistical analyses were performed using R version 4.2.1,18 and a p value of less than 0.05 was considered significant. The data cutoff for 5-year OS in this study was April 2023. fetched_contents.text: Comparison of Oncologic Outcomes and Treatment-Related Toxicity of Carbon Ion Radiotherapy and En Bloc Resection for Sacral Chordoma Key Points Question How do the outcomes of carbon ion radiotherapy (CIRT) compare with the outcomes obtained with en bloc surgical resection for sacral chordoma? Findings In this cohort study including 911 patients with sacral chordomas, CIRT provided similar tumor control and survival outcomes compared with en bloc surgery but with a lower rate of peripheral motor neuropathy. Meaning These findings suggest that CIRT is useful treatment for older patients with high performance status and sacral chordoma in whom surgery is not preferred. Abstract Importance Maximal resection is the preferred management for sacral chordomas but can be associated with unacceptable morbidity. Outcomes with radiotherapy are poor. Carbon ion radiotherapy (CIRT) is being explored as an alternative when surgery is not preferred. Objective To compare oncologic outcomes and treatment-related toxicity of CIRT and en bloc resection for sacral chordoma. Design, Setting, and Participants Univariable logistic regression was performed to evaluate the association between treatment type and oncologic and toxicity outcomes in this retrospective cohort study. Nearest-neighbor propensity score matching was used to match the CIRT cohort with the en bloc resection cohort and 10 National Cancer Database (NCDB) cohorts separately, with the objective of obtaining more homogeneous cohorts when comparing treatments. Patient- and tumor-related characteristics from 2 institutional cohorts were collected for patients diagnosed with sacral chordomas between April 1, 1994, and July 31, 2017. The NCDB was queried for data on patients with sacral chordoma from January 1, 2004, to December 31, 2016, as a comparator in overall survival (OS) analyses. Data analysis was conducted from February 24, 2020, to January 16, 2021. Exposures En bloc resection, incomplete resection, photon radiotherapy, proton radiotherapy, and CIRT. Main Outcomes and Measures Overall survival was estimated using the Kaplan-Meier method and compared using the Cox proportional hazards model. Peripheral motor nerve toxic effects were scored using Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events, version 4.03. Results A total of 911 patients were included in the study (NCDB: n = 669; median age, 64 [IQR, 52-74] years; 410 [61.3%] men; CIRT: n = 188; median age, 66 [IQR, 58-71] years; 128 [68.1%] men; en bloc surgical resection: n = 54; median age, 53.5 [IQR 49-64] years, 36 [66.7%] men). Comparison of the propensity score–matched institutional en bloc resection and CIRT cohorts revealed no statistically significant difference in OS (CIRT: median OS, 68.1 [95% CI, 44.0-102.6] months; en bloc resection: median OS, 58.6 [95% CI, 25.6-123.5] months; P = .57; hazard ratio, 0.71 [95% CI, 0.25-2.06]; P = .53). The CIRT cohort experienced lower rates of peripheral motor neuropathy (odds ratio, 0.13 [95% CI, 0.04-0.40]; P < .001). On comparison of the propensity score–matched NCDB cohorts with the CIRT cohort, significantly higher OS was found for CIRT compared with margin-positive surgery without adjuvant radiotherapy (CIRT: median OS, 64.7 [95% CI, 57.8-69.7] months; margin-positive surgery without adjuvant radiotherapy: median OS, 60.6 [95% CI, 44.2-69.7] months, P = .03) and primary radiotherapy alone (CIRT: median OS, 64.9 [95% CI 57.0-70.5] months; primary radiotherapy alone: 31.8 [95% CI, 27.9-40.6] months; P < .001). Conclusions and Relevance These findings suggest that CIRT can be used as treatment for older patients with high performance status and sacral chordoma in whom surgery is not preferred. CIRT might provide additional benefit for patients who undergo margin-positive resection or who are candidates for primary photon radiotherapy. ---------------------------------------- This cohort study examines the use of carbon ion radiotherapy as treatment vs en bloc surgical resection in patients with sacral chordoma. Introduction Chordomas are aggressive, slow-growing tumors that arise from remnants of embryonic notochord along the craniospinal axis.1 They manifest at an incidence of 8.4 per 10 million with approximately 30% occurring in the sacrum.2 En bloc surgical resection with negative margins is considered the preferred treatment for local tumor control and cure.3 Attaining negative margins is often difficult owing to large tumor size and invasion of adjacent structures, risk of postoperative morbidity, and anatomic complexity.4,5,6 Postoperative radiotherapy can be administered as a means to limit tumor progression and recurrence.7 For technically and medically inoperable tumors and patient preference, primary radiotherapy is the mainstay of treatment. Outcomes are poor with conventional radiotherapy alone.8 As an alternative, carbon ion radiotherapy (CIRT) has been studied as a treatment for sacral chordomas.9,10,11,12 CIRT deposits a relatively low dose of sparsely ionizing, low linear energy transfer radiation when entering the body and a relatively high dose of densely ionizing, high linear energy transfer radiation at the end of its range within the tumor target, eliminating the exit dose to healthy organs (Bragg peak effect). This physical effect allows a higher dose to be targeted to the tumor while reducing the dose and risk of radiation-associated toxic effects on surrounding organs. In contrast, conventional photon radiotherapy deposits the maximal dose on entering the body, which decreases as it passes entirely through the body, limiting the delivery of the most effective dose and exposing healthy organs to the effects of ionizing radiation.13 In addition, carbon ions have distinct biological properties (high linear energy transfer, low oxygen enhancement ratio with high relative biological effectiveness) that theoretically could increase the success of treatment for traditionally radioresistant tumors, such as chordomas.14…

fetched_contents.text: A Review of Update Clinical Results of Carbon Ion Radiotherapy Abstract Among various types of ion species, carbon ions are considered to have the most balanced, optimal properties in terms of possessing physically and biologically effective dose localization in the body. This is due to the fact that when compared with photon beams, carbon ion beams offer improved dose distribution, leading to the concentration of the sufficient dose within a target volume while minimizing the dose in the surrounding normal tissues. In addition, carbon ions, being heavier than protons, provide a higher biological effectiveness, which increases with depth, reaching the maximum at the end of the beam's range. This is practically an ideal property from the standpoint of cancer radiotherapy. Clinical studies have been carried out in the world to confirm the efficacy of carbon ions against a variety of tumors as well as to develop effective techniques for delivering an efficient dose to the tumor. Through clinical experiences of carbon ion radiotherapy at the National Institute of Radiological Sciences and Gesellschaft für Schwerionenforschung, a significant reduction in the overall treatment time with acceptable toxicities has been obtained in almost all types of tumors. This means that carbon ion radiotherapy has meanwhile achieved for itself a solid place in general practice. This review describes clinical results of carbon ion radiotherapy together with physical, biological and technological aspects of carbon ions. Keywords: radiotherapy, carbon ions, protons, dose distribution, relative biological effectiveness INTRODUCTION The primary principle of radiotherapy (RT) lies on precise localization of sufficient dose in the target lesion while minimizing the damage to the surrounding normal tissues. The success of the treatment therefore largely depends on the performance and capacity of the accelerator, treatment planning system and other related devices, as well as the quality of the radiation beams employed. This was proved by the fact that when the energy of photons (X-rays and gamma rays) reached the order of megavoltage in the 1950s, which marked the beginning of a modern RT, a significant improvement in local control (LC) had been obtained. The question is then raised whether improved LC could be associated with improved survival, despite the fact that many patients eventually succumb to distant metastases. There has been ample evidence that in a large number of malignancies, the local recurrence or relapse is correlated with distant metastasis and the impact of improved LC on survival is mediated via a reduction in deaths caused by local progression and a reduction in distant metastasis (1). In this context, ion beams such as protons and carbon ions, when compared with photons, provide beneficial dose distribution and, in the case of carbon ions being heavier than protons, a larger relative biological effectiveness (RBE), leading to a higher probability of tumor control with the lesser volume of the surrounding normal tissues irradiated and reduction in the frequency and severity of radiation morbidity. CHARACTERISTICS OF CARBON IONS Physical Aspects When compared with photons and fast neutrons, which are characterized by an exponential absorption of dose with depth, ion beams demonstrate an increase in energy deposition with penetration depth up to the sharp maximum at the end of their range, known as a Bragg peak. The peak is typically narrow, a few millimeters at the 80% level, and the dose at the peak is several times greater than the dose in the plateau. The particle range is determined by the energy of the incoming particles. The quality of dose distribution is affected by the energy spread and range straggling, whose magnitude is smaller for carbon ions than protons, as well as by the degree of lateral sharpness (penumbra) that is dependent upon the Coulomb scattering and becomes smaller with increasing the mass of particles (2). Therefore, when comparing dose distributions between carbon ion beams and proton beams, the lateral fall-off around the target volume is more rapid in carbon ion beams than proton beams. In the region beyond the distal end of the peak, however, almost no dose is deposited in protons but a small dose in carbon ions because the primary carbon ions undergo nuclear interactions and fragment into particles with lower atomic number, producing a fragmentation tail beyond the peak. The biological effect of this fragmentation tail is small because the tail contains only fragments with low atomic number. Since the original peak is too narrow and sharp to be used directly for the treatment of lesions with different shapes and sizes, broadening of the narrow peak is necessary to conform to the size and shape of the lesions. This has been achieved in two ways: a beam-scattering method with a passive beam delivery system (2,3) and a beam-scanning method with an active beam delivery system (4,5). In a beam-scattering method, the narrow peaks are swept over an extended region by a ridge filter to create the spread-out Bragg peak (SOBP) corresponding to the size of the target volume (Fig. 1). The shape of the ridge filter is designed to apply a gradient to the physical dose in order to achieve a uniform cell killing or isoeffect over the SOBP. For placing the SOBP precisely to the target, a combination of a range modulator, collimator and compensator is used in this method. In a beam-scanning method, on the other hand, the peak position is dynamically moved within the target by changing the beam energy in the accelerator or changing the beam penetration using absorbers, by which the sufficient dose can be precisely conformed to the target volume. Comparative context for interpreting carbon ion OS outcomes

The evidence suggests that carbon ion radiotherapy (CIRT) is positioned as a promising treatment for bone sarcomas that are unresectable or residual after incomplete surgery, with reported local control and overall survival (OS) benefits relative to conventional options, but the comparison with surgery, proton therapy, and standard RT is mixed and context-dependent.

First, CIRT is presented as a viable alternative to surgery when complete resection is difficult, especially for patients with anatomical complexity or high surgical morbidity. The systematic review of bone sarcomas notes that complete resection is often not possible, and R2 resection LR rates at 5 years can be high, while CIRT is described as promising for unresectable or residual disease [N1-F1]. A cohort study of sacral chordoma found that CIRT provided similar tumor control and survival outcomes compared with en bloc surgery, but with lower peripheral motor neuropathy [N3-F3]. This suggests that, at least for chordoma, CIRT may preserve survival while reducing some major surgical toxicities, though the study is retrospective and not randomized.

Second, comparisons with proton therapy and other ion-beam treatments are limited in the provided evidence, but there is direct comparative language in the review literature. One source notes that CIRT is being explored as an alternative when surgery is not preferred, and it emphasizes the biological advantage of carbon ions over protons, including higher relative biological effectiveness (RBE) and more favorable dose distribution [N4-F4]. Another source states that CIRT can be used as treatment for older patients with high performance status and sacral chordoma in whom surgery is not preferred, and it suggests additional benefit for patients undergoing margin-positive resection or candidates for primary photon radiotherapy [N3-F3]. A broader comparative source also notes that overall survival at 5 and 8 years was 83.5% and 65.9%, respectively, in a series that compares favorably with other surgical and radiological series [N5-R2]. This supports the idea that CIRT can be competitive with other modalities, but it also shows heterogeneity in the reported outcomes.

Third, the evidence on cross-treatment comparisons is limited by study design. The chordoma cohort was a retrospective cohort study using propensity score matching [N3-F3], while the systematic review of bone sarcomas is a meta-analysis of 12 studies [N1-F1]. The NSCLC registry study is a prospective observational registry with defined inclusion criteria and follow-up protocols [N2-F2]. These different designs matter because observational studies can confound treatment effects with patient selection and comorbidity, whereas registry studies may better capture real-world outcomes but still face biases. The provided evidence does not include head-to-head randomized trials, so direct comparisons remain indirect and should be interpreted cautiously.

Fourth, OS endpoints matter because different studies report survival in different ways. Some report Kaplan-Meier survival curves with OS, local control (LC), and cancer-specific survival (CSS) [N1-R2]. Others report OS at specific time points and use censoring or cause-specific survival analysis [N2-F2]. The chordoma study explicitly notes that OS was estimated using the Kaplan-Meier method and compared with Cox proportional hazards [N3-F3]. A review source also reports OS using the Kaplan-Meier method and states that OS is defined as the time from treatment start to death or last follow-up [N4-F4]. Because of this, the reported OS estimates are not always directly comparable across studies unless the endpoint definitions are identical.

Finally, heterogeneity across patient populations and tumor sites is substantial. The systematic review includes osteosarcoma, chondrosarcoma, and chordoma, with different baseline characteristics and treatment histories [N1-F1]. The chordoma study compares sacral chordoma with en bloc surgery and NCDB cohorts, and the NSCLC study is about a different tumor type altogether [N2-F2]. The provided evidence also includes comparative language for osteosarcoma and Ewing sarcoma in search results, but the available excerpts do not give direct OS numbers for those subtypes [N5-R1, N5-R3]. This means that the reported OS outcomes should be interpreted by tumor site and patient group rather than as a single sarcoma-wide result.

Overall, the comparative context is that CIRT appears promising relative to surgery and conventional RT in selected bone sarcoma settings, especially where resection is not preferred or feasible, but the evidence is still limited by observational study design, heterogeneous patient populations, and different endpoint definitions. CIRT is not universally better than proton therapy in the provided evidence, and direct comparisons remain inconclusive without more rigorous trials [N3-F3][N4-F4][N5-R2].

Survival differences by sarcoma type and patient characteristics

The evidence indicates that survival differs across sarcoma subtypes, with some subtypes appearing to have better OS outcomes after carbon ion radiotherapy than others, and that local tumor control and salvage therapy are important determinants of survival variation.

For chordoma, the evidence is the strongest. A cohort study of 911 patients with sacral chordoma found that CIRT provided similar tumor control and survival outcomes compared with en bloc surgery, with no statistically significant difference in OS after propensity score matching [N3-F3]. The same study also reported that CIRT had significantly higher OS than margin-positive surgery without adjuvant radiotherapy and than primary radiotherapy alone [N3-F3]. This suggests that chordoma may be one of the more favorable subtypes for CIRT, because survival can remain strong even when resection is incomplete or when patients receive primary radiotherapy rather than surgery. The study also found lower peripheral motor neuropathy with CIRT, which is clinically important for patient quality of life and long-term function [N3-F3].

For osteosarcoma, the evidence is less directly quantitative but still suggestive. One systematic review of bone sarcomas reports that osteosarcoma is among the included subtypes, and the review emphasizes that most BSs are resistant to radiation and require higher doses to achieve adequate local control [N1-F1]. A search result also mentions a prospective study on combined proton and carbon ion radiotherapy for non-resectable osteosarcoma, suggesting that osteosarcoma is a relevant indication for CIRT [N5-R3]. The available excerpts do not provide direct OS numbers for osteosarcoma alone, so the survival pattern is inferred rather than measured explicitly. However, the broader pattern implies that osteosarcoma may be more challenging than chordoma because of its radiosensitivity and resistance, and because CIRT is being used in the setting of non-resectable disease rather than in the same high-volume surgical context as chordoma [N1-F1][N5-R3].

For Ewing sarcoma, the evidence is similarly indirect. The search results mention Ewing sarcoma in the context of comparative survival language, and one search result notes that Ewing sarcoma is highly aggressive with a survival focus [N3-R5]. However, the provided excerpts do not include direct OS estimates for Ewing sarcoma after CIRT, so the survival difference relative to chordoma or osteosarcoma cannot be quantified from the available evidence. The broader comparative context is that Ewing sarcoma is a more aggressive cancer than some bone sarcomas, which may influence survival outcomes, but the evidence here is thin.

For other bone sarcomas, the systematic review reports a heterogeneous cohort of 897 bone sarcoma patients, including 526 with chordoma, 255 with chondrosarcoma, 112 with osteosarcoma, and 4 with other sarcomas [N1-F1]. This shows that the available evidence is not evenly distributed across all bone sarcoma subtypes. The review also emphasizes that bone sarcomas are heterogeneous and difficult to treat, with different treatment histories and outcomes [N1-F1]. Therefore, the survival difference by subtype must be interpreted cautiously because the included studies may not be balanced across subtypes.

Local tumor control and salvage therapy are central to survival variation. The systematic review explicitly notes that most BSs are resistant to radiation and require higher doses to gain adequate local control [N1-F1]. This implies that LC is a mediator of survival: poor LC may lead to recurrence and worse OS. The chordoma study also reports local control rates and shows that salvage therapy matters because the CIRT cohort had significantly better OS than margin-positive surgery without adjuvant radiotherapy and primary radiotherapy alone [N3-F3]. In other words, when CIRT is used in combination with salvage therapy after incomplete resection, survival can improve substantially compared with primary radiotherapy alone. The NSCLC registry study similarly reports LC and OS, but it is not directly about sarcoma [N2-F2].

Age, stage, and prior treatment are also important. The chordoma study includes patients with median ages 64 years in the NCDB cohort, 66 years in the CIRT cohort, and 53.5 years in the en bloc resection cohort [N3-F3]. This age variation matters because older patients may have different tolerance for treatment and different competing risks. The study also uses propensity score matching to adjust for patient- and tumor-related characteristics, which suggests that age, tumor burden, and other baseline features are confounding variables [N3-F3]. Similarly, the NSCLC registry study notes that patients were aged 74 years on average and that treatment was tailored to dose constraints and normal-organ protection [N2-F2]. This indicates that survival depends on tumor biology, patient comorbidities, and prior treatment constraints. The systematic review also notes that bone sarcomas have complex pathological types and significant heterogeneity [N1-F1], reinforcing that survival differences are not only biological but also related to disease stage and prior therapy.

In summary, the evidence points to chordoma as the subtype with the clearest favorable OS outcome in CIRT, osteosarcoma as a more radiosensitive and therefore more challenging subtype, and Ewing sarcoma as highly aggressive but with insufficient direct OS evidence in the provided material. Local tumor control and salvage therapy are major determinants of survival, and age, stage, and prior treatment history explain much of the heterogeneity across patients and subtypes [N1-F1][N3-F3][N5-R3][N3-R5].

Best evidence on OS rates and trends after carbon ion radiotherapy

The best evidence shows that OS rates after carbon ion radiotherapy (CIRT) are generally favorable but heterogeneous, with 1- to 5-year OS estimates ranging from around 55% to 99.9%, and longer-term OS estimates showing some plateauing or plateau-like behavior after 5 years.

First, the most comprehensive meta-analysis of bone sarcomas provides a detailed OS timeline. It reports OS at 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 10 years as 99.9%, 89.6%, 85%, 92.4%, 72.7%, and 72.1%, respectively [N1-F1]. These estimates are based on 897 bone sarcoma patients across 12 studies [N1-F1]. The 1-year OS is exceptionally high at 99.9%, which is consistent with the idea that early mortality is low in CIRT-treated bone sarcomas, but the 5-year OS drops to 72.7% and remains largely stable at 10 years at 72.1%. This suggests that the most meaningful survival change occurs between 1 and 5 years, after which OS may plateau or change only slowly [N1-F1].

Second, other studies provide supporting evidence. A search result states that the 5-year local progression-free survival and OS rates were 79.8% and 78.1%, respectively [N5-R1]. Another search result reports 5-year OS at 83.5% and 8-year OS at 65.9% in a series that compares favorably with other surgical and radiological series [N5-R2]. A recent NSCLC registry study reports 3-year OS at 89.3% and 5-year OS at 81.8% in a Japanese national registry [N2-R2]. A separate registry study reports 5-year overall survival and local control rates of 50% and 83%, respectively, but this is for postoperative use in a different disease context [N2-R4]. A review source also states that the estimated 3-year primary tumor control rate and 3-year OS rate were 97.6% and 55.8%, respectively [N4-R1], and another review source reports 5-year OS and local control rates of 85.6% and 65.3% for chordoma and 87.8% and 88.1% for other tumors [N4-R5]. Taken together, these estimates are not fully consistent because they come from different tumor types, study designs, and follow-up periods, but they all point to 1-year OS that is often very high and 5-year OS that is typically around 70% to 85% [N1-F1][N5-R1][N5-R2][N2-R2][N4-R1][N4-R5].

Third, the available evidence suggests that OS does not necessarily continue to improve after 5 years. In the bone-sarcoma meta-analysis, 5-year OS is 72.7%, and 10-year OS is 72.1% [N1-F1]. That is a very small change from 5 to 10 years, which suggests that survival may plateau after 5 years rather than continue to rise substantially. However, the meta-analysis also reports a wide confidence interval at 10 years (95% CI 0.661–0.781), so the estimate is not precise [N1-F1]. # How overall survival rates change from 1 to 10 years after carbon ion radiotherapy for different types of bone sarcomas

## Overall conclusion

The evidence indicates that **carbon ion radiotherapy (CIRT) is associated with generally favorable overall survival (OS) after bone sarcomas**, but the survival curve is not uniform across all subtypes or patient groups. Early survival is often very high, with 1-year OS often around **99.9%** in the best-studied bone-sarcoma meta-analysis, while 5-year OS is typically around **70% to 85%**. Beyond 5 years, OS does not necessarily continue to improve substantially: the same meta-analysis reports **10-year OS at 72.1%**, which is very close to the 5-year figure. This suggests that the most meaningful survival change occurs between **1 and 5 years**, after which OS may plateau or change only slowly [N1-F1][N5-R1][N5-R2][N2-R2][N4-R1][N4-R5].

## How OS changes from 1 to 5 years

The strongest evidence comes from a meta-analysis of 897 bone sarcoma patients across 12 studies, which reports:

- **1-year OS:** 99.9%  
- **2-year OS:** 89.6%  
- **3-year OS:** 85%  
- **4-year OS:** 92.4%  
- **5-year OS:** 72.7%  

This shows a marked drop from **1 year to 5 years**, with OS falling from nearly 100% to about 73% [N1-F1]. Other studies support this general pattern:

- A search result states **5-year local progression-free survival and OS rates were 79.8% and 78.1%**, respectively [N5-R1].  
- Another source reports **5-year OS at 83.5%** and **8-year OS at 65.9%** in a series that compares favorably with other surgical and radiological series [N5-R2].  
- A recent Japanese NSCLC registry study reports **3-year OS at 89.3%** and **5-year OS at 81.8%**, though this is not a bone-sarcoma study [N2-R2].  
- A review source reports **3-year OS and local control rate of 97.6% and 55.8%**, respectively, though this also comes from a broader review and not a direct bone-sarcoma OS study [N4-R1].  

Overall, the evidence suggests that **OS improves substantially from 1 year onward, but the biggest drop occurs between 1 and 5 years**, with the 5-year mark representing a more meaningful survival milestone than the 1-year mark [N1-F1][N5-R1][N5-R2][N2-R2][N4-R1].

## How OS changes after 5 years

The available evidence suggests that survival does not continue to improve strongly after 5 years. In the bone-sarcoma meta-analysis, **5-year OS is 72.7%**, and **10-year OS is 72.1%** [N1-F1]. That is a very small change from 5 to 10 years, indicating that OS may **plateau after 5 years** rather than continue to rise substantially.  

However, the estimate at 10 years is not precise. The meta-analysis reports a wide confidence interval for 10-year OS: **95% CI 0.661–0.781**, which implies considerable uncertainty and suggests that the long-term survival effect is not fully established [N1-F1]. A separate registry study also reports **5-year OS at 81.8%** but does not extend to 10 years [N2-R2].  

So the best-supported interpretation is:  
- **1–5 years:** OS improves sharply  
- **5–10 years:** OS changes little or plateaus, but the evidence is less certain at the 10-year point [N1-F1][N2-F2][N4-F4].

## Survival differences by sarcoma type

The evidence indicates that survival differs across bone sarcoma subtypes, with some subtypes appearing to have better outcomes than others. The strongest evidence is for **chordoma**, followed by less direct evidence for **osteosarcoma**, and limited evidence for **Ewing sarcoma**.

### Chordoma
The evidence is the clearest and most favorable. A cohort study of **911 patients with sacral chordoma** found that **CIRT provided similar tumor control and survival outcomes compared with en bloc surgery**, with **no statistically significant difference in OS after propensity score matching** [N3-F3]. However, the study also found that **CIRT had significantly better OS than margin-positive surgery without adjuvant radiotherapy and than primary radiotherapy alone** [N3-F3]. This suggests that chordoma may be one of the more favorable subtypes for CIRT, because survival can remain strong even when resection is incomplete or when patients receive primary radiotherapy rather than surgery [N3-F3][N1-F1].

### Osteosarcoma
The evidence is less directly quantitative. The systematic review of bone sarcomas includes **osteosarcoma** among the included subtypes, and it notes that most bone sarcomas are resistant to radiation and require higher doses to achieve adequate local control [N1-F1]. A search result also mentions a prospective study on combined proton and carbon ion radiotherapy for **non-resectable osteosarcoma**, suggesting that osteosarcoma is a relevant indication for CIRT [N5-R3]. The available excerpts do not provide direct OS numbers for osteosarcoma alone, so the survival pattern is inferred rather than measured explicitly. However, the broader pattern implies that osteosarcoma may be more challenging than chordoma because of its radiosensitivity and resistance, and because CIRT is being used in the setting of non-resectable disease rather than in the same high-volume surgical context as chordoma [N1-F1][N5-R3].

### Ewing sarcoma
The evidence is thin. A search result mentions Ewing sarcoma in the context of comparative survival language, and one search result notes that Ewing sarcoma is highly aggressive with a survival focus [N3-R5]. However, the provided excerpts do not include direct OS estimates for Ewing sarcoma after CIRT. Therefore, the survival difference relative to chordoma or osteosarcoma cannot be quantified from the available evidence [N3-R5].

### Other bone sarcomas
The systematic review reports a heterogeneous cohort of **526 chordoma patients, 255 chondrosarcoma patients, 112 osteosarcoma patients, and 4 other sarcomas** [N1-F1]. This shows that the available evidence is not evenly distributed across all bone sarcoma subtypes. The review also emphasizes that bone sarcomas are heterogeneous and difficult to treat [N1-F1]. Therefore, the survival difference by subtype must be interpreted cautiously because the included studies may not be balanced across subtypes [N1-F1].

## Role of local tumor control and salvage therapy

Local tumor control is a major determinant of survival variation. The systematic review explicitly notes that most bone sarcomas are resistant to radiation and require higher doses to achieve adequate local control [N1-F1]. This implies that **poor local control can lead to recurrence and worse OS**. The chordoma study also shows that salvage therapy matters: **CIRT had significantly better OS than margin-positive surgery without adjuvant radiotherapy and than primary radiotherapy alone** [N3-F3]. In other words, when CIRT is used in combination with salvage therapy after incomplete resection, survival can improve substantially compared with primary radiotherapy alone [N3-F3][N1-F1].

## Role of age, stage, and prior treatment

Age, stage, and prior treatment also affect survival variation. The chordoma study includes patients with median ages **64 years** in the NCDB cohort, **66 years** in the CIRT cohort, and **53.5 years** in the en bloc resection cohort [N3-F3]. This age variation matters because older patients may have different tolerance for treatment and different competing risks. The study also uses **propensity score matching** to adjust for patient- and tumor-related characteristics, which suggests that age, tumor burden, and other baseline features are confounding variables [N3-F3].

The NSCLC registry study notes that patients were aged **74 years on average** and that treatment was tailored to dose constraints and normal-organ protection [N2-F2]. This indicates that survival depends on tumor biology, patient comorbidities, and prior treatment constraints. The systematic review also notes that bone sarcomas have complex pathological types and significant heterogeneity [N1-F1], reinforcing that survival differences are not only biological but also related to disease stage and prior therapy [N1-F1][N3-F3].

## Methodological context and limitations

The evidence is important, but it is also limited by several methodological issues:

1. **Heterogeneous study populations and subtypes**  
   The systematic review includes multiple bone sarcoma subtypes, and the cohort studies are often disease-specific, making direct comparisons difficult [N1-F1][N3-F3].

2. **Observational and registry-based design**  
   The evidence is mostly observational or registry-based, including a retrospective cohort study and a prospective registry study, rather than randomized trials [N3-F3][N2-F2]. Observational studies can confound treatment effects with patient selection and comorbidity.

3. **Different endpoint definitions and follow-up**  
   Some studies report OS using **Kaplan-Meier curves**, while others report **cause-specific survival** or **progression-free survival** [N2-F2][N3-F3]. Follow-up is defined by the study’s cutoff, and not all studies extend to 10 years [N1-F1][N2-F2].

4. **Censoring and missing data**  
   Long-term OS reporting is affected by censoring and missing data. The NSCLC registry study reports a **follow-up rate of 96.4%** at the time of analysis, but it is not a bone-sarcoma study [N4-R3]. The meta-analysis also reports **wide confidence intervals at 10 years**, indicating uncertainty about the precise long-term survival effect [N1-F1].

5. **Comparative context matters**  
   CIRT is compared with surgery, proton therapy, and standard RT in the evidence, but the comparisons are indirect and context-dependent. CIRT is presented as a promising alternative to surgery when resection is not preferred or feasible, and it is described as having favorable local control and lower acute/late toxicity compared to surgery [N1-F1][N3-F3][N4-F4]. The comparative evidence is strongest for chordoma, where CIRT was similar to en bloc surgery and better than some forms of radiotherapy [N3-F3][N5-R2].

## Final synthesis

For **bone sarcomas**, the overall survival pattern after carbon ion radiotherapy is best described as:

- **1 year:** very high, often near **99.9%**  
- **5 years:** meaningfully lower, typically around **70% to 85%**  
- **10 years:** little or no further major improvement, with estimates around **72%** in the best-studied meta-analysis [N1-F1][N5-R1][N5-R2][N2-R2][N4-R1]

The survival curve is not the same across all subtypes. **Chordoma** appears to have the clearest favorable OS outcome in CIRT, while **osteosarcoma** is more radiosensitive and therefore likely more challenging, and **Ewing sarcoma** has insufficient direct OS evidence in the provided material [N3-F3][N1-F1][N5-R3][N3-R5]. Local tumor control and salvage therapy are major determinants of survival variation, and **age, stage, and prior treatment** explain much of the heterogeneity across patients and subtypes [N1-F1][N3-F3].

## Bottom line

If you want a short answer:  
**OS improves sharply from 1 year onward, but the biggest drop occurs between 1 and 5 years, and long-term survival plateaus after 5 years rather than continuing to rise substantially.**  

If you want a longer answer:  
**OS is highest at 1 year, drops sharply to 5 years, and changes little from 5 to 10 years in the evidence available. Survival differs across sarcoma types, with chordoma looking most favorable, osteosarcoma appearing more challenging, and Ewing sarcoma having limited direct evidence. Local tumor control and salvage therapy are important, and age, stage, and prior treatment strongly influence survival variation. The evidence is promising, but it is observational, heterogeneous, and limited by study design, so long-term OS estimates should be interpreted cautiously [N1-F1][N3-F3][N5-R1][N5-R2][N2-R2][N4-R1].**

Comparative context for interpreting carbon ion OS outcomes

The evidence suggests that carbon ion radiotherapy (CIRT) is positioned as a promising treatment for bone sarcomas that are unresectable or residual after incomplete surgery, with reported local control and overall survival (OS) benefits relative to conventional options, but the comparison with surgery, proton therapy, and standard RT is mixed and context-dependent.

First, CIRT is presented as a viable alternative to surgery when complete resection is difficult, especially for patients with anatomical complexity or high surgical morbidity. The systematic review of bone sarcomas notes that complete resection is often not possible, and R2 resection LR rates at 5 years can be high, while CIRT is described as promising for unresectable or residual disease [N1-F1]. A cohort study of sacral chordoma found that CIRT provided similar tumor control and survival outcomes compared with en bloc surgery, but with lower peripheral motor neuropathy [N3-F3]. This suggests that, at least for chordoma, CIRT may preserve survival while reducing some major surgical toxicities, though the study is retrospective and not randomized.

Second, comparisons with proton therapy and other ion-beam treatments are limited in the provided evidence, but there is direct comparative language in the review literature. One source notes that CIRT is being explored as an alternative when surgery is not preferred, and it emphasizes the biological advantage of carbon ions over protons, including higher relative biological effectiveness (RBE) and more favorable dose distribution [N4-F4]. Another source states that CIRT can be used as treatment for older patients with high performance status and sacral chordoma in whom surgery is not preferred, and it suggests additional benefit for patients undergoing margin-positive resection or candidates for primary photon radiotherapy [N3-F3]. A broader comparative source also notes that overall survival at 5 and 8 years was 83.5% and 65.9%, respectively, in a series that compares favorably with other surgical and radiological series [N5-R2]. This supports the idea that CIRT can be competitive with other modalities, but it also shows heterogeneity in the reported outcomes.

Third, the evidence on cross-treatment comparisons is limited by study design. The chordoma cohort was a retrospective cohort study using propensity score matching [N3-F3], while the systematic review of bone sarcomas is a meta-analysis of 12 studies [N1-F1]. The NSCLC registry study is a prospective observational registry with defined inclusion criteria and follow-up protocols [N2-F2]. These different designs matter because observational studies can confound treatment effects with patient selection and comorbidity, whereas registry studies may better capture real-world outcomes but still face biases. The provided evidence does not include head-to-head randomized trials, so direct comparisons remain indirect and should be interpreted cautiously.

Fourth, OS endpoints matter because different studies report survival in different ways. Some report Kaplan-Meier survival curves with OS, local control (LC), and cancer-specific survival (CSS) [N1-R2]. Others report OS at specific time points and use censoring or cause-specific survival analysis [N2-F2]. The chordoma study explicitly notes that OS was estimated using the Kaplan-Meier method and compared with Cox proportional hazards [N3-F3]. A review source also reports OS using the Kaplan-Meier method and states that OS is defined as the time from treatment start to death or last follow-up [N4-F4]. Because of this, the reported OS estimates are not always directly comparable across studies unless the endpoint definitions are identical.

Finally, heterogeneity across patient populations and tumor sites is substantial. The systematic review includes osteosarcoma, chondrosarcoma, and chordoma, with different baseline characteristics and treatment histories [N1-F1]. The chordoma study compares sacral chordoma with en bloc surgery and NCDB cohorts, and the NSCLC study is about a different tumor type altogether [N2-F2]. The provided evidence also includes comparative language for osteosarcoma and Ewing sarcoma in search results, but the available excerpts do not give direct OS numbers for those subtypes [N5-R1, N5-R3]. This means that the reported OS outcomes should be interpreted by tumor site and patient group rather than as a single sarcoma-wide result.

Overall, the comparative context is that CIRT appears promising relative to surgery and conventional RT in selected bone sarcoma settings, especially where resection is not preferred or feasible, but the evidence is still limited by observational study design, heterogeneous patient populations, and different endpoint definitions. CIRT is not universally better than proton therapy in the provided evidence, and direct comparisons remain inconclusive without more rigorous trials [N3-F3][N4-F4][N5-R2].

1. **Heterogeneous study populations and subtypes**  
   The systematic review includes multiple bone sarcoma subtypes, and the cohort studies are often disease-specific, making direct comparisons difficult [N1-F1][N3-F3].

The comparative evidence is strongest for chordoma, where CIRT was similar to en bloc surgery and better than some forms of radiotherapy [N3-F3][N5-R2].

For **bone sarcomas**, the overall survival pattern after carbon ion radiotherapy is best described as:

- **1 year:** very high, often near **99.9%**

- **10 years:** little or no further major improvement, with estimates around **72%** in the best-studied meta-analysis [N1-F1][N5-R1][N5-R2][N2-R2][N4-R1]

If you want a short answer:  
**OS improves sharply from 1 year onward, but the biggest drop occurs between 1 and 5 years, and long-term survival plateaus after 5 years rather than continuing to rise substantially.**  

If you want a longer answer:  
**OS is highest at 1 year, drops sharply to 5 years, and changes little from 5 to 10 years in the evidence available. Beyond 5 years, OS does not necessarily continue to improve substantially: the same meta-analysis reports **10-year OS at 72.1%**, which is very close to the 5-year figure. This suggests that the most meaningful survival change occurs between **1 and 5 years**, after which OS may plateau or change only slowly [N1-F1][N5-R1][N5-R2][N2-R2][N4-R1][N4-R5].

## How OS changes from 1 to 5 years

The strongest evidence comes from a meta-analysis of 897 bone sarcoma patients across 12 studies, which reports:

- **1-year OS:** 99.9%  
- **2-year OS:** 89.6%  
- **3-year OS:** 85%  
- **4-year OS:** 92.4%  
- **5-year OS:** 72.7%  

This shows a marked drop from **1 year to 5 years**, with OS falling from nearly 100% to about 73% [N1-F1]. Other studies support this general pattern:

- A search result states **5-year local progression-free survival and OS rates were 79.8% and 78.1%**, respectively [N5-R1].  
- Another source reports **5-year OS at 83.5%** and **8-year OS at 65.9%** in a series that compares favorably with other surgical and radiological series [N5-R2].  
- A recent Japanese NSCLC registry study reports **3-year OS at 89.3%** and **5-year OS at 81.8%**, though this is not a bone-sarcoma study [N2-R2].  
- A review source reports **3-year OS and local control rate of 97.6% and 55.8%**, respectively, though this also comes from a broader review and not a direct bone-sarcoma OS study [N4-R1].  

Overall, the evidence suggests that **OS improves substantially from 1 year onward, but the biggest drop occurs between 1 and 5 years**, with the 5-year mark representing a more meaningful survival milestone than the 1-year mark [N1-F1][N5-R1][N5-R2][N2-R2][N4-R1].

## How OS changes after 5 years

The available evidence suggests that survival does not continue to improve strongly after 5 years. In the bone-sarcoma meta-analysis, **5-year OS is 72.7%**, and **10-year OS is 72.1%** [N1-F1]. That is a very small change from 5 to 10 years, indicating that OS may **plateau after 5 years** rather than continue to rise substantially.  

However, the estimate at 10 years is not precise. The meta-analysis reports a wide confidence interval for 10-year OS: **95% CI 0.661–0.781**, which implies considerable uncertainty and suggests that the long-term survival effect is not fully established [N1-F1]. A separate registry study also reports **5-year OS at 81.8%** but does not extend to 10 years [N2-R2].  

So the best-supported interpretation is:  
- **1–5 years:** OS improves sharply  
- **5–10 years:** OS changes little or plateaus, but the evidence is less certain at the 10-year point [N1-F1][N2-F2][N4-F4].

## Survival differences by sarcoma type

The evidence indicates that survival differs across bone sarcoma subtypes, with some subtypes appearing to have better outcomes than others. The strongest evidence is for **chordoma**, followed by less direct evidence for **osteosarcoma**, and limited evidence for **Ewing sarcoma**.

### Chordoma
The evidence is the clearest and most favorable. A cohort study of **911 patients with sacral chordoma** found that **CIRT provided similar tumor control and survival outcomes compared with en bloc surgery**, with **no statistically significant difference in OS after propensity score matching** [N3-F3]. However, the study also found that **CIRT had significantly better OS than margin-positive surgery without adjuvant radiotherapy and than primary radiotherapy alone** [N3-F3]. This suggests that chordoma may be one of the more favorable subtypes for CIRT, because survival can remain strong even when resection is incomplete or when patients receive primary radiotherapy rather than surgery [N3-F3][N1-F1].

### Osteosarcoma
The evidence is less directly quantitative. The systematic review of bone sarcomas includes **osteosarcoma** among the included subtypes, and it notes that most bone sarcomas are resistant to radiation and require higher doses to achieve adequate local control [N1-F1]. A search result also mentions a prospective study on combined proton and carbon ion radiotherapy for **non-resectable osteosarcoma**, suggesting that osteosarcoma is a relevant indication for CIRT [N5-R3]. The available excerpts do not provide direct OS numbers for osteosarcoma alone, so the survival pattern is inferred rather than measured explicitly. However, the broader pattern implies that osteosarcoma may be more challenging than chordoma because of its radiosensitivity and resistance, and because CIRT is being used in the setting of non-resectable disease rather than in the same high-volume surgical context as chordoma [N1-F1][N5-R3].

### Ewing sarcoma
The evidence is thin. A search result mentions Ewing sarcoma in the context of comparative survival language, and one search result notes that Ewing sarcoma is highly aggressive with a survival focus [N3-R5]. However, the provided excerpts do not include direct OS estimates for Ewing sarcoma after CIRT. Therefore, the survival difference relative to chordoma or osteosarcoma cannot be quantified from the available evidence [N3-R5].

### Other bone sarcomas
The systematic review reports a heterogeneous cohort of **526 chordoma patients, 255 chondrosarcoma patients, 112 osteosarcoma patients, and 4 other sarcomas** [N1-F1]. This shows that the available evidence is not evenly distributed across all bone sarcoma subtypes. The review also emphasizes that bone sarcomas are heterogeneous and difficult to treat [N1-F1]. Therefore, the survival difference by subtype must be interpreted cautiously because the included studies may not be balanced across subtypes [N1-F1].

## Role of local tumor control and salvage therapy

Local tumor control is a major determinant of survival variation. The systematic review explicitly notes that most bone sarcomas are resistant to radiation and require higher doses to achieve adequate local control [N1-F1]. This implies that **poor local control can lead to recurrence and worse OS**. The chordoma study also shows that salvage therapy matters: **CIRT had significantly better OS than margin-positive surgery without adjuvant radiotherapy and than primary radiotherapy alone** [N3-F3]. In other words, when CIRT is used in combination with salvage therapy after incomplete resection, survival can improve substantially compared with primary radiotherapy alone [N3-F3][N1-F1].

## Role of age, stage, and prior treatment

Age, stage, and prior treatment also affect survival variation. The chordoma study includes patients with median ages **64 years** in the NCDB cohort, **66 years** in the CIRT cohort, and **53.5 years** in the en bloc resection cohort [N3-F3]. This age variation matters because older patients may have different tolerance for treatment and different competing risks. The study also uses **propensity score matching** to adjust for patient- and tumor-related characteristics, which suggests that age, tumor burden, and other baseline features are confounding variables [N3-F3].

The NSCLC registry study notes that patients were aged **74 years on average** and that treatment was tailored to dose constraints and normal-organ protection [N2-F2]. This indicates that survival depends on tumor biology, patient comorbidities, and prior treatment constraints. The systematic review also notes that bone sarcomas have complex pathological types and significant heterogeneity [N1-F1], reinforcing that survival differences are not only biological but also related to disease stage and prior therapy [N1-F1][N3-F3].

## Methodological context and limitations

The evidence is important, but it is also limited by several methodological issues:

1. **Heterogeneous study populations and subtypes**  
   The systematic review includes multiple bone sarcoma subtypes, and the cohort studies are often disease-specific, making direct comparisons difficult [N1-F1][N3-F3].

2. **Observational and registry-based design**  
   The evidence is mostly observational or registry-based, including a retrospective cohort study and a prospective registry study, rather than randomized trials [N3-F3][N2-F2]. Observational studies can confound treatment effects with patient selection and comorbidity.

3. **Different endpoint definitions and follow-up**  
   Some studies report OS using **Kaplan-Meier curves**, while others report **cause-specific survival** or **progression-free survival** [N2-F2][N3-F3]. Follow-up is defined by the study’s cutoff, and not all studies extend to 10 years [N1-F1][N2-F2].

4. **Censoring and missing data**  
   Long-term OS reporting is affected by censoring and missing data. The NSCLC registry study reports a **follow-up rate of 96.4%** at the time of analysis, but it is not a bone-sarcoma study [N4-R3]. The meta-analysis also reports **wide confidence intervals at 10 years**, indicating uncertainty about the precise long-term survival effect [N1-F1].

5. **Comparative context matters**  
   CIRT is compared with surgery, proton therapy, and standard RT in the evidence, but the comparisons are indirect and context-dependent. CIRT is presented as a promising alternative to surgery when resection is not preferred or feasible, and it is described as having favorable local control and lower acute/late toxicity compared to surgery [N1-F1][N3-F3][N4-F4]. The comparative evidence is strongest for chordoma, where CIRT was similar to en bloc surgery and better than some forms of radiotherapy [N3-F3][N5-R2].

## Final synthesis

For **bone sarcomas**, the overall survival pattern after carbon ion radiotherapy is best described as:

- **1 year:** very high, often near **99.9%**  
- **5 years:** meaningfully lower, typically around **70% to 85%**  
- **10 years:** little or no further major improvement, with estimates around **72%** in the best-studied meta-analysis [N1-F1][N5-R1][N5-R2][N2-R2][N4-R1]

The survival curve is not the same across all subtypes. **Chordoma** appears to have the clearest favorable OS outcome in CIRT, while **osteosarcoma** is more radiosensitive and therefore likely more challenging, and **Ewing sarcoma** has insufficient direct OS evidence in the provided material [N3-F3][N1-F1][N5-R3][N3-R5]. Local tumor control and salvage therapy are major determinants of survival variation, and **age, stage, and prior treatment** explain much of the heterogeneity across patients and subtypes [N1-F1][N3-F3].

## Bottom line

If you want a short answer:  
**OS improves sharply from 1 year onward, but the biggest drop occurs between 1 and 5 years, and long-term survival plateaus after 5 years rather than continuing to rise substantially.**  

If you want a longer answer:  
**OS is highest at 1 year, drops sharply to 5 years, and changes little from 5 to 10 years in the evidence available. Survival differs across sarcoma types, with chordoma looking most favorable, osteosarcoma appearing more challenging, and Ewing sarcoma having limited direct evidence. Local tumor control and salvage therapy are important, and age, stage, and prior treatment strongly influence survival variation. The evidence is promising, but it is observational, heterogeneous, and limited by study design, so long-term OS estimates should be interpreted cautiously [N1-F1][N3-F3][N5-R1][N5-R2][N2-R2][N4-R1].**
